    memoryPressure:
        When the machine runs out of memory, the operating system ends the
        program using it rather than Suspense. Every child process the
        application starts, and everything those start in turn, a run
        target's build, a task's harness and the commands it runs on the
        host, piton, git, and each container, is marked as the one to end
        first, and Suspense itself is never marked so, so a heavy build that
        uses up memory is what the system ends, never the window holding the
        user's work.

        On Linux, each child process is started with its `oom_score_adj` set
        to 1000, written to `/proc/self/oom_score_adj` in the child just
        before it runs its program, so it and all it starts inherit it, and
        each container is run with `--oom-score-adj=1000`; Suspense keeps its
        own as it was given, never raising it. Where the system runs
        systemd, each run target and each task on the host also runs in a
        transient user scope of its own, as `systemd-run --user --scope`
        gives, so the system\'s out-of-memory handling ends that scope and
        not Suspense\'s. On macOS and Windows, which give no such control,
        each child runs in a process group or job object of its own, as a
        run target already does, so a child ended for its memory takes
        nothing with it, and Suspense keeps running.

        A child ended for running out of memory says so: a run target reads
        "Ran out of memory" in its error colour, and a task or a spec build
        fails saying the process was ended because the machine ran out of
        memory, naming the program, as its exit by SIGKILL with the system
        recording an out-of-memory kill shows, rather than only its exit
        status. The debug log records it the same way.

EOF

content.text:
I added a "Memory Pressure" section to `ApplicationScope`. When the machine runs out of memory, the operating system should end the heavy child process, such as a Rust build, instead of Suspense. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 82 files.

- **Linux:**
  - Every child process starts with `oom_score_adj` set to 1000, which everything it starts inherits, and containers run with `--oom-score-adj=1000`. That marks them to be ended first.
  - Suspense leaves its own score as it was given.
  - Where systemd is present, run targets and host tasks also run in their own user scope (`systemd-run --user --scope`), so the system's memory handling ends that scope and not Suspense.
- **macOS and Windows:** they give no equivalent control. Each child runs in its own process group or job object, so a child killed for memory takes nothing else with it and Suspense keeps running.
- **Reporting:**
  - A run target killed this way reads "Ran out of memory" instead of a bare exit code.
  - A task or spec build fails saying the machine ran out of memory, naming the program.
  - The debug log records it the same way.

The systemd scope is my addition, and it only helps where systemd is present.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `ApplicationScope` `#memory-pressure` and `#child-processes`, `RunTargetsScope` `#stopping`, and `ContainerEnvironmentScope` `#description`.
